content.title: Artemis II: 4 astronauts launch for 10-day moon mission
content.text: (NewsNation) — Artemis II, the first crewed mission to the moon in more than five decades, took off Wednesday evening, sending four astronauts on a historic 10-day mission. NASA’s last crewed mission to the moon, Apollo 17, launched in December 1972. Nearly 54 years later, astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen embarked on an expedition meant to pave the way for a future lunar base. NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket, topped with its Orion crew capsule, roared to life just before sunset at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The thunderous ascent left behind a towering column of thick white vapor. This is a great start and a great first step.” He said Artemis II is the logical extension of what NASA has been doing in recent decades — sending crews to the International Space Station to adapt to Low Earth orbit. “Now, we’re going to transform the space station, if you will, to the lunar surface. So, we’re going to send crews back and forth on a regular basis to learn how to live and work on the moon,” he said. That, in turn, potentially gets NASA closer to one day sustaining human life on Mars, Anderson said. Originally scheduled for a February takeoff, the Artemis II launch was delayed by ongoing repairs and hydrogen fuel leaks. Now, it’s just up to the weather. “Things are looking really good for the launch,” she said. Infographic shows the flight path of the Artemis II fly-around mission, set to launch on April 1. (Credit: NASA) The mission’s four astronauts — three Americans and one Canadian — have been in quarantine for the past week, ensuring that everyone on the flight is healthy ahead of their long-awaited mission. “They’ve spent the better part of three years learning every system on this spacecraft … I think their nervousness is calmed down just by their intimate knowledge of the spacecraft and this mission that’s ahead of them,” Korth said. Artemis II launch: What is a lunar fly-by mission? Video Player is loading.Current Time 0:00Duration 0:00Artemis II launch: Moon fly-by will send astronauts 250K miles into space | Morning in America Artemis II launch: Moon fly-by will send astronauts 250K miles into space | Morning in America NOW PLAYINGArtemis II launch: Moon fly-by will send astronauts 250K miles into space | Morning in America The crew members will pilot the Artemis to the moon, where they will “check out some of our new systems” on the craft. The mission will allow NASA to determine whether the aircraft is working successfully and whether the technology is prepared for expected launches in the coming years. In February, NASA’s new administrator, Jared Isaacman, announced a scheduling change for the agency and the new goal of having astronauts land on the moon by 2028. As part of the new schedule, NASA plans to revise Artemis III’s mission profile to allow an Orion spacecraft to launch in 2027, when it will rendezvous with the program’s human landing system. The following year, Artemis IV will launch — and take over its predecessor’s mission of making a moon landing, Isaacman said. There is potential for at least two landings in 2028 and for a future “moon base” to be built, he said during a news conference. “Everybody agrees this is the only way forward,” he said. Wednesday’s launch was not without minor glitches. Battery issue surfaces before launch The “closeout crew” resolved a last-minute issue of a battery with a temperature that was out of range. They determined it was a sensory issue that would not affect the launch. Hatch is ‘now closed,’ NASA announces “The hatch is now closed. The Artemis II astronauts are now strapped into their seats and ready for launch,” NASA announced with about an hour before the launch window begins. Artemis II crew boards the Orion The Artemis II astronauts have boarded the Orion capsule, getting in place for the upcoming moon mission. “Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy are taking their seats atop the most powerful manned rocket ever built,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote in a post on X. “They have trained for years for this moment, and now they are preparing to execute a mission that will take us back around the Moon and begin the next chapter of human space exploration.” Issue with Artemis’ ‘flight termination system’ resolved Just hours before launch, officials said there was an issue with Artemis II’s “flight termination system,” which is related to the range capacity of the rocket. It did not scrap the launch. After troubleshooting the issue, officials announced at 5:15 p.m. EST that it is resolved. Reuters contributed to this report.
